A short list of promises that are always kept builds a reputation that no amount of charm can match. Before every yes, she suggested, Leo should ask himself one plain question: can I really do this by then?

When a customer asked for a quick repair that afternoon, Leo felt the old yes rising in his throat like a hiccup. He swallowed it, and said instead that he would check the stockroom and telephone by four o'clock with an honest answer. The customer blinked, then smiled, and Leo saw that she seemed to trust him more for having refused to guess.

In the stockroom Leo counted his spare inner tubes, checked the parcel book and read through the work list from top to bottom before he allowed himself to name a day. The honest answer turned out to be Wednesday, which sounded less impressive than Monday but had the one great advantage of being true. A date given in this way, he discovered, feels solid underfoot, like a plank rather than a rumour.

At four o'clock exactly, with one eye on the shop clock, Leo picked up the telephone and gave the customer his honest answer. She was so astonished that she laughed aloud and said that in all her years nobody had ever called back when they said they would. It was a small thing, and yet he put the receiver down feeling as tall as a lighthouse.

That evening Leo leaned on the garden wall and told Ada, a little shyly, that keeping one small promise had felt surprisingly good. Trust begins exactly there, she replied, not with grand gestures or fine speeches but with one kept word, and then another, and then another. She went back to her pots, and Leo understood that the lesson had only just started.

A few days later Nell's bicycle chain snapped halfway down Harbour Road, and she wheeled the machine into the shop and asked whether it could be mended before six the next morning. Leo felt the old yes climbing his throat, warm and automatic and wildly unwise, and he glanced at the work list pinned above the bench. There were already four bicycles ahead of hers, and two of them belonged to people who had been waiting a week.

“I can't do six,” Leo told her, “because I would have to push someone else's bicycle aside, and that would not be fair to either of you.” “What I can do is bring it to your door by noon, and I will keep to that.” Nell looked at him for a second, as if he had changed colour, and then said that noon would be fine, and that she had expected worse.

Outside the shop, Bram from the hardware store asked whether Leo could service three family bicycles by the following morning, as a favour between neighbours. Leo smiled, shook his head gently, and offered to do one that afternoon and the other two early the next week. Bram looked mildly surprised and then perfectly happy, which suggested that the dreaded refusal had been far larger in Leo's imagination than in the world.

A kind no, Ada told Leo, has three parts, and none of them is an apology for existing. You thank the person for asking, you say clearly what you cannot do, and then you offer whatever you honestly can, even if it is small. Vagueness is the unkind option, she added, because it leaves the other person to guess whether to wait.

Leo's sister Ines telephoned on Thursday evening to ask whether he could mind her craft stall at the Sunday market, and the old Leo would have groaned inwardly and said yes. This time he told her warmly that Sundays were his only day of real rest, that he loved her very much, and that he could lend her his folding table and a flask of tea. There was a short silence on the line, then a laugh, and she said that it was a fair offer.

Mira asked whether she might leave an hour early on Friday for her brother's school concert, and Leo checked the list before answering. He could manage perfectly well without her, so he said yes, and he was surprised by how different it felt to give an answer he truly meant. The same word, he realised, can be a burden or a gift, depending on whether anything honest stands behind it.

Leo had always believed, without ever looking at the belief, that saying no would make people dislike him. Three weeks of honest refusals had produced no such result: Nell still brought him buns, Bram still nodded across the street, and Kemal had begun to drop in simply to chat. Fear, he noted, is a great artist, and it had painted a monster on a wall where there was only a coat.

A customer asked Leo to leave the worn brakes on her bicycle alone, in order to keep the bill small, and the old Leo would have shrugged and agreed. He held up the thin, shiny brake pad and explained gently that he could not send her down the hill on it, however much he wished to save her money. A no, he saw, can be the most honest kindness of all, especially when it protects someone from a quiet danger.

Two days later the customer returned, wheeling her bicycle and wearing a smile that had no trace of resentment in it. The new brakes, she said, made the machine feel like a completely different animal, and she thanked Leo for declining the easy answer. He thought of all the times he had said yes to avoid a moment of awkwardness, and how little those yeses had ever earned him.

Leo noticed that his evenings had become quieter, and that the telephone in his head, which used to ring with unkept promises long after closing time, had fallen almost silent. Fewer promises, he found, meant fewer worries, and the ones he did make were so solid that he could rest his whole weight upon them. When he told Ada, she nodded slowly and said that the first card had a way of paying back its owner.

After dropping a whole box of spokes across the floor, Leo caught sight of his tired reflection in the shop window and heard himself mutter that he was useless. He said it as casually as one remarks on the weather, in a tone he had been using for so long that he no longer heard it. Ada, who happened to be passing the window with her shopping bag, heard it perfectly well.

Ada stepped inside, set down her basket among the spilled spokes, and asked him a simple question. Would he ever speak those words to a friend, she wanted to know, or to a customer who had made exactly the same mistake? Leo opened his mouth to say of course not, and then understood that this was her entire point.

For one whole day Leo listened to the voice in his own head, and the results made him wince. Before lunch he had called himself stupid, hopeless and typical, and had said more unkind things than he would have allowed a rude customer to say about him. The cruelty was so quiet and so familiar that it had never occurred to him to object.

Ada wrote two sentences side by side on a scrap of card: I made a mistake, and I am a mistake. The first, she said, is an honest description that points towards a repair, while the second is a verdict that points nowhere and happens to be false. Rule one, she reminded him, asks us to mean what we say, and that includes the things we say when nobody else is in the room.

Leo ruined the first wheel he tried to straighten that afternoon, and the old words rose up in his mouth like a well-worn habit. He stopped, set the wheel down, and said aloud that this one had gone wrong and that he would simply do it again. The second attempt took ten minutes, and he suspected that it went better because he was no longer working with an enemy at his shoulder.

By the fence at the back of the bakery, Bram and Nell were whispering about Gus, who ran the café on the corner and had closed it twice that month without explanation. Leo felt the familiar pull of belonging, the sense that one small joke at Gus's expense would instantly make him part of the circle. He had always thought of gossip as harmless warmth, like standing near a stove.

Bram turned and asked Leo what he thought was going on with Gus, and the question hung in the air like an invitation. Leo said, with perfect honesty, that he did not know and that the best way to find out would be to ask the man himself. Then he went back to work, a little pink in the face, and the whispering behind him stopped as if a window had been closed.

On the Gull, Ada recalled, a rumour once ran along the quay about a young deckhand, a tale about missing money that was entirely untrue and was passed on mostly out of boredom. It took the best part of a year for people to look him in the eye again, she said, and by then he had given up the sea and gone to work inland. Words said behind a person's back, she added, have a way of arriving ahead of them.

When Bram admired a beautifully true wheel hanging from the ceiling, Leo told him at once that Mira had built it, and that she was the finest wheel builder he had ever worked beside. She was in the other room and could not possibly hear, and that, he realised, was the whole point. Praise offered behind a person's back, he thought, is the kind that can be trusted.

Later that afternoon Leo told Mira directly, with no joke to soften it, that her wheels were the best he had ever seen. She went pink to the tips of her ears and mumbled that it was only practice, but she worked for the rest of the day with her head held a fraction higher. Meaning what you say, he saw, includes the kind things you mean and have never said.

Leo bought a small blue notebook from the stationer's and wrote the word Promises across the top of the first page. Then he made himself a promise about the notebook itself: every time he gave his word, he would write it down at once. It was an unglamorous system, with no charts or colours, but a promise written down, he reasoned, is much harder to lose than one that merely floats in the air.

On Tuesday afternoon Leo finished a repair that he had promised for four o'clock, wheeled the bicycle out to the pavement, and put a neat tick in the notebook with the stub of a pencil. The pleasure was small but definite, like the quiet click of a well-fitted lock, and it lingered all the way back to the bench. For years he had treated the end of a job as the moment to start worrying about the next one, and he had never once paused to enjoy having kept his word.

By the end of the week the notebook held six promises and six ticks, and nothing at all in the column marked sorry. It was not a long list, which was precisely the point, because every item on it was something that Leo had checked he could do before he said so. He closed the book feeling lighter than he had in years, like a man who had finally put down a heavy and entirely unnecessary bag.

Leo had promised a customer called Sam a new pair of wheels for his daughter's bicycle by Saturday, her birthday, and had checked and double-checked that it was possible. Then, on Wednesday, a storm tore through the district, closed the coast road and stopped Pavel's van somewhere miles away behind a fallen tree. For the first time since the notebook began, a tick was in danger, and it was not Leo's carelessness that had put it there.

Leo could have waited and hoped that the van would somehow arrive, but he understood that hope, in this case, would only be a polite word for hiding. A promise that cannot be kept, he decided, should be reported at once, while the other person still has time to make other plans. He picked up the telephone on Thursday morning, before his courage could leak away.

Leo told Sam plainly that the wheels would not arrive in time for Saturday, that the cause was a storm and not a mistake, and that he was truly sorry. Then he offered what he could actually do: a loan bicycle of the right size, polished and ready, for the birthday itself. He did not make a single excuse that was not also a fact, and he felt his hands relax on the receiver as he spoke.

Sam was audibly disappointed, but he thanked Leo before the call ended, and the warmth in his voice was real. Because he knew on Thursday, he said, he still had two days to plan, and a late announcement on Saturday morning would have spoiled a day that mattered very much to his daughter. Bad news, Leo saw, is far easier to forgive when it arrives with time attached.

On Saturday the birthday girl wobbled gleefully up and down her street on the loan bicycle, with a ribbon tied to the handlebar and no idea that anything had gone wrong. On Monday the coast road reopened and Pavel's van arrived at last, and Leo fitted the new wheels that very afternoon and delivered the bicycle to her door with his own hands. Sam shook his hand for a little longer than people usually do, and he did not say very much.

Kemal dropped into the shop for no reason except to say hello, and he noticed the small blue notebook open beside the till. He had heard, he said, how Leo had telephoned Sam early about the wheels, and in a district as small as this one a kept word travels almost as fast as a broken one. He bought a new bell that he did not strictly need, as a kind of vote of confidence.

Ada set the first card face up in the middle of her kitchen table, where it would stay while they talked about the next one. Rule one, she said, does not make a person trusted overnight, and anyone who promises otherwise is selling something; it builds trust slowly, one kept promise at a time. Leo looked at the card and found, to his surprise, that it already seemed to belong to him.

On Monday a customer called Hale marched into the shop with a crumpled bill in his fist, his face the colour of a ripe tomato. He slapped the paper on the counter and announced, at a volume that made Mira look up from the back room, that the price was nothing short of robbery. Leo felt his own face grow hot, and something inside him closed like a fist.

There was no pause in Leo, no gap at all between the heat and the words, and he heard himself snap that Hale could take his custom somewhere else if the price was so offensive. For a moment the two men glared at each other across the counter like cats on a wall. Then Hale snatched up his bill, turned on his heel, and slammed the door so hard that the bell jangled for several seconds.

The bell was still swinging when Leo realised that his hands were shaking and that his heart was banging like a loose shutter. Mira stood in the doorway of the back room and said nothing at all, though her silence was far from empty. He had spent weeks learning to keep his promises, and in one hot moment he had thrown all that patience across the counter like a spanner.

Leo looked up Hale in the ledger and found that he had been a customer for more than six years, with never an unpaid bill or a harsh word. Then he checked the invoice and discovered that the price of the part really had jumped since Hale's last visit, so that the man's outrage, though badly delivered, had not been entirely unreasonable. The anger had spoiled a conversation that would have cost nothing to hold well.

Ada drew a wave on a paper napkin, with a steep rise, a sharp peak and a long slope down the other side. Anger behaves just like this, she explained, climbing quickly and reaching its height within moments, and then, if nobody feeds it, slowly beginning to fade. The trouble is almost never the anger itself but what we say and do at the very top of the wave.

In rough water, Ada told him, a sensible captain never wrenches the wheel, because a hard turn at the wrong moment can put a ferry on its side. She had learned to make small and gentle corrections, letting the boat answer slowly, and she had found that the same approach worked on people. A wave of anger, she said, is not a signal to turn the wheel but a signal to hold it steady.

Ada tapped the napkin just below the peak of the wave with the tip of her pencil. One slow breath, she said, is often long enough for the top of the wave to begin falling away, and that small drop is the difference between a reply you regret and one you can stand behind. It is not much to ask, and it costs nothing, which is probably why people ignore it.

Leo asked what on earth he should do about Hale, and Ada, instead of handing him a script, said that the first task was to learn the pause. Only a calm mind can repair a damaged conversation, she said, and a mind still smoking from the last explosion will usually start another. Mending, in her experience, goes much better on the second day than on the first.

Ada reached into her cardigan pocket and produced the second card, which she held up in the lamplight as though it were a small and rather important lantern. Take one breath before you answer, it said, in the same plain upright letters as the first, and it looked even smaller than the rule before it. That, Leo was beginning to suspect, was the secret of Ada's rules: they were too modest to be argued with.

Surely one breath is not enough, Leo said, turning the card over as though the answer might be printed on the back. One is enough to begin, Ada replied, and beginning is the hardest part of any habit, so there is no sense in asking for more yet. When you can manage one every single time, she added with a smile, we shall talk about two.

After closing, Leo stood alone in the quiet shop with one hand resting on his chest, feeling slightly foolish. He breathed in slowly while he counted to four, and out more slowly still while he counted to six, as Ada had shown him at her kitchen table. The first few attempts were clumsy, and his mind wandered to spokes and invoices, but he kept going until the room seemed to grow larger.

A long, slow breath out, Ada explained, helps the body to settle, because the same body that races when we are cross can also be coaxed back towards calm. It is not magic, she was careful to add, and it will not solve a single problem on its own, but it gives the thinking part of us a chance to arrive. Anger without a breath, she said, is rather like a horse that has lost its reins on a steep and crowded hill.

A customer asked the same question about gears for the fifth time, and Leo felt his jaw tighten and the old heat begin to climb his neck. He took one slow breath, in for four and out for six, and when he spoke his voice was level and almost cheerful. The customer, who had clearly been braced for a sigh, relaxed visibly, and the fifth answer turned out to be the one that finally stuck.

Mira noticed that Leo seemed to be breathing very slowly behind the counter, with a look of intense concentration, and she asked whether he was feeling quite well. When he explained, a little embarrassed, she laughed and said that she did exactly the same thing before every examination. The shop, it seemed, had been full of secret breathers all along, and nobody had thought to compare notes.

On his Sunday walk through the park, Leo came to a fork in the path and found himself stopping, almost without meaning to, to decide which way to go. It struck him that a pause is exactly such a place, a fork between reacting and choosing, where the road you take is no longer decided for you by habit. Both paths led to the lake in the end, but the walk, he noticed, would feel entirely different depending on which he picked.

On the bus into town Leo watched a tired stranger rub his eyes, check his phone, and sigh the long sigh of someone carrying more than he can manage. It occurred to Leo that when people speak sharply, they are very often reporting on their own weather rather than on anything he has done. The thought did not excuse rudeness, but it made it considerably easier to pause before answering it.

A customer came in out of the rain, shook her umbrella with unnecessary violence, and snapped that everything in this town had become ridiculously expensive. Leo felt the familiar sting, then took a breath, and in the space it made he understood that her bad mood had arrived long before she opened the door. He asked whether she would like a cup of tea while he looked at her tyre, and her face changed completely.

Ada warned Leo not to mistake the pause for a sulk, a silent punishment, or a clever way of walking out of an argument. It lasts about as long as a single breath, she said, and when it is over you must still answer, honestly and clearly, because the aim is to speak well and not to avoid speaking. A pause that never ends, she added, is not wisdom or patience but merely a closed door.

Ines telephoned that evening, and it soon became clear that she was still a little hurt about the market stall. Leo's first instinct was to defend himself with a long list of reasons, but he took a breath, put the list aside, and let her finish. When she had said everything, she sounded lighter, and she even thanked him for the folding table, which had been a great success.

That evening Leo turned to a clean page in his notebook and wrote the heading Breaths, followed by a tally that came to eleven. Two of them had arrived too late to help, and one had been little more than a sigh, but the other eight had changed what he said, and therefore what happened next. It was a modest score, he thought, but it was entirely his own, and it was a good deal better than none.

On Thursday morning Leo's phone buzzed with a notification, and he opened it to find a new online review of the shop with a single lonely star. Overpriced, it said, and the owner is rude, and the writer would not recommend the place to anyone. The words were few, but they landed like stones in a pond, and the ripples spread through his whole day.

Heat flooded Leo's face, and his thumbs began to move over the screen before his mind had a chance to catch up. In half a minute he had written three furious sentences, each one more cutting than the last and each one perfectly justified, and his finger hovered above the button marked send. The cursor blinked at him, patient and neutral, like a traffic light in the middle of the night.

The second card rose in his mind, small and white and stubborn, and Leo took one long breath, in for four and out for six. Then he deleted every word of the reply, one letter at a time, and laid the phone face down on the counter as if putting a sleeping animal to bed. It was astonishing how much lighter the shop felt without that little weight in his hand.

The next morning, with a cup of tea beside him and the heat long gone, Leo read the review again and noticed what he had been too angry to see: the writer was Hale. Seen calmly, the complaint about the price had a grain of truth in it, and the word rude, though it hurt, was an accurate description of how Leo had behaved on that Monday. It is remarkably hard to stay angry with a mirror, however unflattering the reflection happens to be.

Leo wrote a short reply, read it twice as though he were its recipient, and changed one word that sounded defensive. He thanked Hale for the feedback, admitted without ornament that he had been rude on Monday, explained that the maker had raised the price of the part, and offered to check the bicycle for free. Nothing in it was a trick or a tactic, which was the secret of its strength.

Mira read the reply over his shoulder, and her eyebrows rose slowly until they disappeared beneath her fringe. A month ago, she said, she would have expected something short, hot and probably involving capital letters, and she was not at all sure that she would have blamed him. Then she smiled and said that she was glad the old Leo had not been in charge that morning.

Three days later the shop bell jangled, and Hale stood in the doorway pushing his bicycle, his shoulders stiff and his expression that of a man who would rather be anywhere else on earth. Leo's heart gave a single hard knock, and then he took one slow breath and let the wave rise and fall. Whatever came next, he told himself, he would answer it with something he meant.

Leo laid the supplier's price list on the counter and explained, step by step, why the part had cost so much more this time, and he did not hurry and did not sigh. Hale read the figures twice, grunted, and asked two sensible questions, which Leo answered with the same unhurried patience. It was, he reflected, a perfectly ordinary conversation, and it was extraordinary how close it had come to never happening.

Hale cleared his throat, stared at the counter, and admitted that he had been angry at the bill and not at Leo, and that he had written the review in the heat of a bad week. Leo said that he had been angry too, and that the difference between them was only that Hale had written his anger down. They shook hands across the counter, and both men looked slightly relieved to have something to do with their arms.

That evening Leo's phone buzzed once more, and he opened it to find that Hale had changed his review to four stars. The owner, it now said, listens, and puts things right, which is rarer than it should be. Leo read the line three times, then closed the phone and went to the back door to tell Ada, who was already at the wall with the kettle.

Pavel delivered a long crate of frames that Leo had been waiting for since the storm, and when it was opened every single one turned out to be the wrong size. Leo took his slow breath, in for four and out for six, but this time it barely touched the heat, which went on climbing like water in a kettle. The second card, it seemed, had a limit, and he had just reached it.

Leo remembered what Ada had mentioned in passing about the days when a single breath is not enough: that it is no shame to leave the room. He told Mira, in a voice that was almost level, that he needed ten minutes and would be back, and he walked out of the door before he could say something he would regret. It was not running away, he told himself, but the opposite: it was refusing to be run away with.

Leo walked the length of the harbour wall with a bottle of cold water in his hand, letting the wind from the bay push against his chest. With every few steps the heat drained a little further out of his shoulders, until the crate of wrong frames shrank from a catastrophe to a problem. Walking, he discovered, is simply a way of breathing with the whole body, and the cure works best outdoors.

Out on the bay the horn of the Gull sounded, deep and unhurried, and Leo found that he was smiling. He thought of Ada standing at that wheel for forty years, through fog and gales and difficult passengers, and he felt that a crate of wrong frames was a small thing to be shipwrecked by. A problem looks quite different, he thought, when it is placed next to something as vast as the sea.

Back at the shop, Leo telephoned the supplier, and for the first time in his working life he asked a question before making an accusation. Together with Pavel, who stayed on the line from his van, he traced the error to a label that had been misread in the warehouse, hundreds of miles from either of them. Nobody had been careless or dishonest, and had Leo shouted, he would have owed several people an apology.

The next day Pavel arrived in person with the correct frames, loaded the wrong ones back into the van without being asked, and said that most customers would have shouted at him for an hour. He had a long list of customers, he added, and he found himself delivering to Leo's door a little earlier than the others. A calm word, it seemed, is paid back in small and unexpected ways, usually when one is not looking.

For years Leo had kept a small wooden comment box beside the door, and for years he had been too nervous to open it. One evening, with a lamp and a mug of tea, he emptied it onto the desk and sorted the cards into two piles: those that told him something he could use and those that were only noise. It was uncomfortable work, but it was oddly freeing to realise that criticism, once sorted, is far less frightening than criticism in the dark.

The useful pile contained two good ideas that had been sitting there for months: a seat for people who wait, and earlier opening on Saturdays. The noise pile held a few insults, a drawing of a moustache, and a card that said only bicycles are a silly invention. Leo bought a small cushioned bench that week, and he put the moustache drawing, which was rather good, on the wall.

Ada read a few of the cards, chuckled at the moustache, and gave Leo a question to ask of any criticism: is any of it true, and is any of it useful? Whatever passes both tests, she said, should be kept and acted upon with gratitude, and whatever fails them can be allowed to float away like a paper boat. The pause that Leo had learned for anger, she pointed out, works just as well for the sting of a hard word.

Ada laid the second card on top of the first, and the two sat neatly together like a pair of old friends. Between what we feel and what we say, she told him, there is a small gap, and the whole of our freedom lives inside it. Leo thought of the fork in the park path, and of Hale's four stars, and he found that he had no wish to argue.

On Sunday evening Leo sent Mira a friendly message asking whether she could work an extra afternoon that week, and then he sat looking at the screen as though it might change its mind. No answer came that night, and none arrived the next morning, though he checked his phone seven times before he had finished his breakfast. Silence, he found, is a very noisy thing when you are the one waiting.

Mira arrived on Monday afternoon looking pale and distracted, and she checked her phone twice before she had even taken off her coat. She said nothing at all about his message, not even a word of apology, and Leo watched her from across the shop with his arms folded and his face growing stiffer by the minute. The old heat began to stir, but this time it came with a story attached.

By three o'clock Leo had decided that Mira was angry with him, and his mind, always an eager author, had supplied the reason: the afternoon last week when he had spoken to her sharply about a missing spanner. By four he was sure that she was planning to look for another job, and by five he had mentally advertised for her replacement. Not one of these dramatic conclusions rested on a single fact, and every one of them felt completely true.

All afternoon Leo answered Mira only in short, cold sentences, convinced that he was being dignified and that she must be feeling guilty. At four she picked up her bag, said that she had to leave, and slipped through the door before he could find a reply. The bell behind her sounded smaller than usual, and the shop felt too large for one person.

That night Leo lay awake and stared at the ceiling while his thoughts circled like gulls over a harbour. The mind abhors an empty space, and where it has no facts it will happily supply a story, which is almost always a worse one than the truth. He rehearsed three speeches, each more dignified and more unfair than the last, and fell asleep at about the time the bakery lights came on.

On Tuesday morning Ada listened to the whole tale over the garden wall, with her head tilted like a thoughtful bird, and then asked a plain question. What exactly are the facts, she wanted to know, and what has your mind added since? Leo thought hard and was forced to admit that the facts could be written on a postage stamp: he had sent a message, and no reply had come.

Ada told him about a morning on the Gull when a pale passenger stood at the rail, silent and hunched, for most of the crossing. She had decided that he must be in some terrible trouble, and she had spent the whole journey planning how to console him. When she finally went to speak to him, he turned green, apologised, and was sick over the side, and her tragedy turned out to be a stomach.

Ada fetched a notepad and drew a line down the middle of the page, with facts on one side and stories on the other. Leo's column of facts held a single line, while the column of stories ran on to the bottom and had to be continued over the page. It was a humbling arrangement, and also a strangely comforting one, because nobody can be heartbroken by a blank space where the evidence should be.

The mind fills every gap, Ada said, in the way a person finishes a jigsaw with pieces from the wrong box, forcing them in until the picture looks complete. A guess may feel certain, may even feel like knowledge, but it remains a guess until someone has asked. Leo, whose own jigsaw currently featured a resentful Mira and an empty workbench, felt rather ashamed of the artwork.

Ada took the third card from her pocket and slid it across the table, where it lay beside the small stack of the others like a little white door. Ask before you decide what is true, it said, in the same patient handwriting. It was the simplest rule yet, and Leo was beginning to understand that simplicity was exactly what made them hard.

On Wednesday morning Leo unlocked the shop in the grey light and felt the old story tugging at his sleeve, insisting that he already knew the answer. He decided to ask Mira directly, and he practised the words aloud between the tyres and the toolbox, trying to find a version that sounded curious rather than accusing. It was a strange thing to rehearse, since the whole point of a question is that you do not know what comes back.

When Mira arrived that afternoon, Leo took one slow breath, in for four and out for six, and asked his question as gently as he knew how. He said that he had sent her a message on Sunday, that he had not heard back, and that he was not sure it had reached her. He kept his arms unfolded and his voice open, and the words came out sounding almost like what he truly felt, which was concern.

Mira pulled her phone from her pocket and held it up, and Leo saw that the screen was a spider's web of cracks around a black and lifeless centre. It had fallen from her bicycle basket on Sunday afternoon, she explained, and she had not seen a single message since, which was why she had checked it so anxiously and why she had been so quiet. She had been too embarrassed to say that she could not afford the repair yet.

Leo burst out laughing, partly from relief and partly from pure embarrassment, and had to sit down on the nearest stool. For two whole days he had nursed a dignified grievance against a woman whose only crime was to drop her phone, and the elaborate story he had built was now no more than a puff of smoke. He told Mira the whole thing, including the imagined advertisement for her replacement, and she laughed until she cried.

A good question, Ada told him, is simple, curious and open, and it leaves a door ajar for the answer to walk through. It asks what happened and what the other person needs, rather than demanding to know why they did something, which tends to make people defend themselves before they have spoken. The best questions, she added, are the ones you honestly want to hear answered.

When Mira arrived ten minutes late one morning, Leo felt the old accusation rise, the sharp why are you late that had once come so readily to his tongue. He swallowed it and asked instead what had happened that morning, in the tone of someone who actually wanted to know. It turned out that she had walked her small brother to school because their mother was ill, and the lateness, seen from the inside, looked like kindness.

Leo laid his phone face down on the counter, folded his hands, and listened to Mira's answer from beginning to end without once reaching for the next thing to say. He had always treated other people's sentences as obstacles between him and his reply, and it was a surprise to discover how much lay in the middle and at the end of them. Listening, he realised, is asking a question for the second time, with your whole attention.

A customer marched in and complained for a full minute about the gears Leo had adjusted the week before, and the old Leo would have interrupted somewhere around the fifteenth second. This time he listened until she had run out of breath, nodded, and asked what she most needed him to do. It turned out that she wanted neither a refund nor an apology, only a five-minute adjustment and the feeling that someone had heard her.

A second habit began to grow out of the first, which was to say back what he had heard before acting on it. So you need it by Thursday, he would say, and the brakes matter more than the paint, and people would either nod with relief or correct him on the spot. Either way, he had saved himself a wrong turn, and both of them knew that they had understood each other.

Leo showed Ada the new page in his notebook, headed Questions, with a column of tidy ticks beneath it. The more you ask, she said, the less you have to guess, and the less you guess, the fewer battles you will fight with people who were never your enemies. She handed back the notebook as carefully as if it were a small and valuable animal.

As the days grew longer, Saturdays became busier and busier, and Leo badly needed another pair of hands. Instead of saying so, he sighed theatrically, glanced at the clock, and murmured that it was all rather a lot, as though hoping that Mira would read the message in the air. She nodded sympathetically, went on sweeping, and left at the usual time, completely unaware that she had been asked anything.

Leo decided that the kindest thing was to be clear, so he wrote a short note and handed it to Mira before she had taken off her coat. Could you work on Saturday mornings in March, it said, because the shop will be busy and I need you; if you cannot, please tell me honestly. It struck him that this was the first time he had asked for help without apologising for existing.

Mira read the note twice, looked up, and said that she would be happy to work the Saturday mornings in March, since nobody had ever asked her so plainly before. In return she asked for the first Friday afternoon of each month off, for her brother's school meetings, and they shook on it across the counter. A clear question, Leo noticed, invites a clear answer, and a clear answer is a much better foundation than a hopeful silence.

On the Gull, Ada recalled, there had been a deckhand so proud that he never asked anyone to share the heavy mooring ropes, and one cold morning he strained his back lifting one alone. She would have taken the other end in a moment, she said, if only she had known, and nothing in his silence had told her. People are generally willing to help, she added, but they cannot read minds, and neither could she, even as captain.

Leo asked Pavel whether he could write down the delivery days and rough times for the coming month, explaining that it would help him to make honest promises to customers. Pavel looked pleasantly startled, scribbled a neat table on the back of an envelope, and said that nobody had asked him that in eleven years of driving. For the first time Leo knew when each parcel would arrive, and his promises became firmer as a result.

Leo was about to quote a customer the price of a set of brake cables when he noticed that the figure on his laptop did not match the figure in the paper catalogue beside it. One of them had to be wrong, but he had no way of knowing which, and the old Leo would have chosen the lower one and hoped for the best. It occurred to him that asking, in this case, meant asking a second source.

Leo telephoned the supplier and simply asked which of the two prices was correct, a question that took eleven seconds to put and saved him a good deal of embarrassment. The paper catalogue, it emerged, was a year old and had been superseded by the figures on the laptop, which meant that his customer would have been quoted far too little. Checking, he reflected, is really just asking a question in a different outfit, and it pays for itself.

On a crowded train, Leo noticed a stranger frowning in his direction and felt the old story begin to assemble itself: the man disliked him, the man thought him rude, the man was about to say something. Instead he labelled the idea a guess, put it on a shelf in his mind, and went back to watching the fields go by. When the stranger rose to leave, he apologised for the bump of his rucksack and smiled, and the frown, it seemed, had been concentration.

When a stranger walked into the shop looking harassed and impatient, Leo met her with an open smile and a first guess that she probably meant well. It was not blind trust, he reminded himself, but a starting point that he was prepared to test, and to change if the evidence turned against it. A generous first guess, he was discovering, costs nothing and often improves the evidence.

Leo asked, as lightly as he could, whether he might help her find something, and the woman's whole face softened with relief. She was not rude in the least, only lost, and a little late for a meeting at Gus's café, which she had been looking for up and down Harbour Road for twenty minutes. Leo walked her to the corner and pointed, and the guess that she was a difficult customer drifted off like smoke.

On Monday Bram announced to anybody who would listen that the council meant to close Harbour Road for a whole week in the spring, and by lunchtime the news had passed from shop to shop, growing slightly with each telling. Nell talked of ruined deliveries, Gus of empty tables, and Leo found himself calculating the loss of a week's customers on the back of an envelope. It was remarkable how real a rumour could become before anyone had checked it.

Leo felt the pull of the calculation and then remembered the third card, so he put down the envelope and telephoned the council to ask. After being passed between two cheerful and bewildered clerks, he learned that only the pedestrian crossing near the bridge would close, for two days, in the middle of the following month. He thanked them, wrote the dates in his notebook, and walked down the street to share the good news.

Leo gathered Bram, Nell and Gus outside the bakery and told them exactly what the council had said, reading the dates from his notebook. Bram went the colour of a boiled beetroot, Nell laughed so hard that she dropped a tray of rolls, and a little cloud of worry lifted from the whole of Harbour Road. Nobody was blamed, but a few people looked thoughtfully at their own habit of repeating things they had not checked.

Ines had not telephoned for nearly a week, and the old Leo would have invented a quarrel to explain it, a missed birthday or a careless remark. Instead he picked up the phone and asked her, quite simply, how she was and whether anything was wrong. She had been in bed with a cold, she said, and had been too sniffly to talk, and she was delighted that he had asked.

Ada warned Leo that asking is not the same as interrogating, and that a person who is questioned three times about the same thing begins to feel accused. Ask once, she said, kindly and with real interest, and then believe the answer you are given, unless there is a very good reason not to. A question is an offer of trust, and it is spoiled when it arrives with a magnifying glass.

Sometimes the answer to a question is simply, I don't know, and Leo learned to receive it with thanks. He remembered how often he had invented answers himself rather than admit ignorance, and he saw that an honest I don't know is a gift, because it leaves the situation exactly as clear as it really is. People also relax noticeably when they find that nobody is going to punish them for it.

On a tricky Thursday a customer demanded a repair by noon while a delivery ran late and the telephone rang without pause. Leo checked his list before he promised anything, took a breath before he spoke, and asked her what she really needed the bicycle for. The answer turned out to be a whole day more flexible than the demand, and the three rules, he noticed, had begun to work together like the legs of a stool.

Mira leaned on the counter at closing time and observed that the shop felt different these days, quieter and kinder, and that Leo did too. He thanked her, and said honestly that he was only trying, and that he still got it wrong more often than anyone would guess. She said that this, in her experience, was exactly how people described the things they were getting right.

Ada laid the third card on the stack and set a smooth grey stone on top of the three, as if to stop them flying away in the wind. Rule three, she said, replaces worry and guessing with something far gentler: a short and honest question, asked at the right moment. Leo noticed that the stone had a small white stripe running through it, and he wondered what sea it had come from.

Ada picked up the last card, turned it face down, and held it against her chest like a card player with a promising hand. The fourth rule, she said, was not quite like the other three, because those concerned how Leo meets the world, whereas this one concerned what he leaves behind him. He would receive it soon, she assured him, and she was a woman who honoured her promises.

In April a huge delivery of spring stock buried the shop floor under cardboard boxes, packing paper and loose tools, until only a narrow path remained between the door and the counter. Leo stood on the threshold with a clipboard in his hand and felt the old overwhelm rising, the thick, drowsy sense that nothing he did could possibly make a difference. Mira, who was due in an hour, would find him in exactly the same spot.

Leo lowered himself onto a stool in the middle of the chaos and simply sat there, looking at the boxes as a man looks at a mountain. There was so much to do that he could not identify a first step, and the lack of a first step paralysed him more completely than any amount of work could have done. Ten minutes passed in this paralysis, and somewhere out in the sunny street a bicycle bell rang, cheerful and quite irrelevant.

Ada picked her way between the boxes with a flask under her arm, surveyed the scene without comment, and poured two mugs of tea. She did not offer advice; she asked, in the mildest tone possible, where Leo would begin if he had only five minutes. It was exactly the sort of question that Leo had learned to treat with respect, and it had the same effect as opening a window.

Ada turned over the last card at last and laid it on a cleared corner of the workbench, where it caught the light from the window. Leave every place a little better than you found it, it said, and beneath the line, in smaller letters, she had added the words and every person. Leo read it, looked at the boxes, and understood why she had saved it for this particular morning.

Ada tapped the word little on the card with the tip of her pencil, and then she tapped it again. The rule, she said, does not ask for a perfect shop, or a perfect anything, because perfection is a cruel master and a very poor guest. It asks only for a place that is a little better than it was a moment ago, and anyone, she added, can manage a little, which is always enough to begin.

Leo began, since there was nowhere else to begin, with the workbench: he cleared it, wiped it until the old scratches shone, and hung every tool on its proper hook on the wall board. The rest of the shop was exactly as chaotic as before, but one small corner had changed its character completely, and he found that he kept glancing at it, as at a lit window. A single clean surface, he noticed, makes the rest of the mess look temporary.

Leo set the kitchen timer for five minutes and cleared a single shelf, stacking the new tyres in tidy rows with their labels facing outward. When it rang, he found to his surprise that he did not want to stop, because the neat shelf had changed his sense of what was possible. Like Ada's tea, it made the next step visible, and the next step is almost always the whole difficulty.

Ada pointed out that the rule does not care how small the act is, so long as it leaves something slightly better: one spanner returned to its hook, one email answered, one bin emptied before it overflows. Small acts have an unfair reputation, she said, because nobody applauds them and everybody benefits from them. A shop, like a ship, is kept afloat mainly by things that nobody notices being done.

When Mira arrived she stopped in the doorway, stared at the transformed corner, and then, without a word, picked up the bicycle pumps and hung them in a neat row on the wall. It was remarkable how quickly one person's small improvement gave another person permission to make a second one. By the end of the afternoon the two of them had cleared half the floor, and had talked more than they had worked.

At closing time the shop was by no means perfect, and half of the boxes still stood in the corner waiting for the morning. It was, however, noticeably better than it had been at dawn, and that, Leo realised, was precisely what the card had asked and nothing more. He hung the key on its hook beside the door, patted the wall as one pats a horse, and went home with an unusually light step.

Week by week Leo tidied one more shelf, one more drawer, one more forgotten corner, never attempting anything heroic. The small improvements piled up quietly, like coins in a jar, until one morning he arrived to find that the shop looked like a different and much more capable place. Nobody had made a speech, and no great clean-up day had been announced; it had simply happened a little at a time.

Each evening Leo spent ten minutes leaving the shop a little better than he had found it: the floor swept, the till counted, the day's tools wiped and returned to their places. In the morning he no longer had to rescue the shop before he could begin work, and he noticed that he was less tired at nine than he had been at noon. Kindness to his future self, he found, had turned out to be wonderfully practical as well as pleasant.

Before he left each evening, Leo laid out the tools for the first job of the following day, in the order he would need them, with the bicycle already on the stand. It was a small gift to the person who would walk through the door at eight o'clock, a person who happened to be himself and who was always grateful. He switched off the lamp, and the bench waited in the dark like a table laid for breakfast.

Mornings, once the most stressful part of Leo's day, became surprisingly peaceful, and he found that he was beginning to look forward to unlocking the door. The sun came in across a clear bench, the first job was waiting with its tools beside it, and nothing in the room was shouting for his attention. He had the odd, unfamiliar sensation of being on time for his own life.

An elderly customer called Dilys wheeled in a bicycle with a bell that squeaked like a mouse in distress, and apologised for taking up his time over something so small. Leo, who a few months earlier would have glanced at the clock, put down his work, oiled the little mechanism, and made it ring as clear as a church on a Sunday. He did not charge her, since it had taken him two minutes and given him a great deal of pleasure.

Dilys rang the bell twice, laughed aloud, and told Leo that he had just made her whole day better, which was no small achievement for a man with a spanner. He suddenly understood the small letters on the card, the ones that said and every person, and he saw that a shop can be tidied in more than one sense. A kind word, a clear answer, a bell that rings properly: all of these leave someone a little better off.

Over a cup of tea on the new bench, Dilys explained that the bicycle had belonged to her husband, who had been gone for eight years. She rode it to the harbour every Sunday morning because it felt like keeping him company, and Leo listened with his whole attention. Then, without asking whether it was necessary, he cleaned the machine from handlebar to rear wheel until it gleamed, because some repairs are not about bicycles at all.

On his way to work one morning Leo noticed a drift of crisp packets and paper cups against the bicycle rack on Harbour Road, which was not his rack and not, strictly speaking, his problem. He picked them all up and carried them to the bin, which took less than two minutes, and the street looked at once as if somebody cared. Nobody saw him do it, and he was pleasantly surprised to find that this made no difference at all.

On a cold, drenched morning Leo carried a mug of hot tea out to Pavel, who was unloading parcels from his van in a downpour with rain running off the end of his nose. Pavel took it in both hands, closed his eyes for a moment, and said that it was the best thing that had happened to him all week. It had cost Leo a minute and a teabag, and the exchange rate struck him as ridiculously generous.

Standing in the doorway at the end of a long and happy afternoon, Leo watched the people go by along Harbour Road and reflected on how many of them passed through his small shop in the course of a year. Each of them left with a slightly better day or a slightly worse one, and he realised that he had more say in which it was than he had ever imagined. The thought made his small shop feel important, and the work of every ordinary day feel worth doing well.

The rack was wobbly, rusty and ugly, but it was not Leo's, so he remembered the third card and telephoned the council to ask whether he might mend it. They said yes at once, thanked him with an enthusiasm that suggested nobody had ever rung before, and sent round a tin of green paint and a wire brush. He stood on the pavement turning the tin in his hands, delighted by how easy asking had been.

On Sunday morning Leo scrubbed the rust from the rack with the wire brush, and within half an hour he had company. Nell appeared with a tray of warm buns, and Bram arrived with a spanner and a suspiciously innocent expression. By ten o'clock three neighbours were working side by side, arguing cheerfully about the correct shade of green, and the rack was beginning to look like a small public work of art.

A girl wheeling a bicycle with a flat tyre stopped to watch the work and asked, rather shyly, whether anyone could show her how to mend a puncture. Leo knelt on the pavement beside her, took the wheel, and showed her every step: levers, tube, patch and pump, each stage explained in plain words. She did it again herself while he watched, and her face when the tyre held was something he would remember for a long time.

Leo had an idea that he could not shake off: a free puncture clinic, two hours on the first Saturday of every month, where anyone could learn to mend their own tyre. Before he told a single person, however, he sat down with Mira and the calendar, because the first card had taught him to promise only what he could really deliver. Together they looked at the work list, the opening hours and the stock, and they agreed that it was possible.

Ten children arrived for the first clinic on a bright and breezy Saturday, some of them with bicycles, some with parents and one with a very large dog. Leo began, as the third card had taught him, by asking what they most wanted to learn, and he wrote every answer on a board: punctures, brakes, chains, and how to stop a bell rattling. It turned out that children, unlike adults, will tell you precisely what they need.

When the inner tube burst for the second time, a small boy flung his tyre lever across the pavement and declared that bicycles were stupid and so was he. Leo knelt beside him and, without a lecture, showed him how to breathe in for four and out for six, counting quietly together. The third attempt worked, and the boy's grin, when the tyre held, was larger than the whole street.

Month by month the puncture clinic grew, until twenty children and a small forest of bicycles crowded the pavement outside the shop on the first Saturday of each month. Ada watched it all from the garden wall with a mug between her hands, saying nothing, and wearing the expression of a captain who has seen her ship handed to a competent crew. When Leo glanced up and caught her eye, she lifted the mug an inch, which for Ada was a standing ovation.

One Saturday Kemal arrived at the clinic with his young niece, a tool roll under his arm, and the air of a man with a quiet purpose. He had been practising on his own bicycle all spring, he said, and it seemed only right to pass the knowledge on. Leo remembered the dark Friday when Kemal had stood in the same doorway with a disappointed face, and the two men grinned at each other without needing a word.

A father arrived at the clinic with three broken bicycles and the cheerful hope that they could all be mended for nothing. Leo thanked him warmly, explained that the clinic was for teaching rather than repairing, and offered a fair price for the work at the shop on Monday, with the date written down. The father looked slightly taken aback, then nodded, and Leo saw that a kind no was still, even after all these months, a muscle that needed regular exercise.

Ada slid the fourth card onto the stack, set the grey stone on top of all four, and patted it as if it were the head of a loyal dog. Rule four, she said, does not ask anyone to change the world, only to leave their own corner of it a little better, and the world has always been improved mostly in this way. Leo thought of the rack, the clinic and Dilys's bell, and he found that the pile of cards looked rather like a foundation.

On a Tuesday in late summer the alarm clock failed, and Leo woke an hour late with a dry mouth and a head full of unfinished arguments. He skipped breakfast, forgot his notebook, and hurried to the shop with one shoelace trailing, so that the day began on the back foot and stayed there. Even the early sunshine seemed a little too bright, and rather unfairly cheerful for the mood of the morning.

At nine o'clock a customer asked for a rush repair by two, and Leo, flustered and anxious to make up for his bad start, heard the old yes leap out of his mouth. The notebook was at home, the work list was unread, and the first rule lay forgotten like a coin from another country. He had broken it in less than two seconds, and the damage would not show for hours.

At noon Mira reported, as gently as she could, that the part for the rush repair was not in stock, and Leo snapped at her in a voice he had not used for months. The words were out before any breath had a chance to intervene, and he saw her flinch, a small hurt movement, like a door closing a few inches. It was the second rule, broken in the space of an afternoon, while the wave was at its peak.

At three a customer came back with the wrong part, and Leo decided in an instant that she had been careless when she ordered it, and told her so in a tone of weary superiority. A minute later, checking the order form to prove his point, he found his own handwriting on it, with the wrong number written in. He had skipped the third card entirely, and the third card had caught him anyway.

By closing time Leo was too tired and ashamed to do anything but get out, and he left tools scattered across the bench, the floor unswept and the till uncounted. He locked the door a little too hard, walked home with his head down, and did not stop to say goodnight to anyone, not even to the gulls. It was the fourth rule, broken at the end of a day that had broken the other three.

That night Leo sat on the edge of his bed with his head in his hands and told himself that he always did this. Nothing had changed, he thought, and all those weeks of effort had been no more than a charming little story. Then he heard, in the quiet of the room, the very words he had once muttered to the shop window, and he recognised them as untrue then and no truer now, merely louder.

Unable to sleep, Leo wandered out into the back yard, where he found Ada perched on the garden wall in a long dressing gown with a mug of cocoa, apparently waiting for him. He told her all of it: the false yes, the snapped word, the unjust accusation and the untidy bench. When he had finished, he braced himself for disappointment, and instead she began, very gently, to laugh.

The rules are not an examination, Ada told him, and nobody is marking you; they are a compass, and a compass is never cross with a traveller for wandering off the path. All that matters is how soon you look at it again, and whether you take the next step in the right direction. Anyone who keeps the rules perfectly, she added with a twinkle, is either a saint or a liar.

The next morning Leo arrived early, made Mira a cup of tea before she could take off her coat, and told her plainly that he was sorry for snapping at her and that it had been unfair. He then telephoned the customer from the day before, admitted that the paperwork mistake had been his and not hers, and offered to put it right at his own cost. Starting again turned out to be mostly a matter of saying what was true.

That morning Leo copied the four rules in his own cramped handwriting onto four white cards and laid them in a row on his workbench in the early sun. Looking at them side by side, he saw how they leaned on one another: a promise is easier to keep after a breath, a breath is easier after a question, and everything is easier in a tidy place. They were not four rules but one small way of living, read from left to right.

It was October again, a full year since that tangled Friday, and the leaves were blowing along Harbour Road in the same careless way. Leo, locking up one evening, realised that he could not remember when he had last felt the old dizzy sense of being overwhelmed, and that the shop had become known for bicycles mended on the day they were promised. He had not become a different man, he thought, only a slightly better organised one, with a very good notebook.

Mira told Leo, one slow afternoon, that she wanted to stay at the shop for another year at least, and that she wished to take over the wheel building completely. She had also begun to teach him her trick for centring a rim, a delicate skill at which he proved a slow but eager pupil. It was a strange and happy reversal to be taught by the person he had once feared he was about to lose.

One Saturday morning a girl of seventeen called Tess stood in the doorway holding a folded note, and she looked as if she would turn and run at the slightest provocation. She had helped her little cousin at the puncture clinic earlier that year, she explained, and had never forgotten the feeling of mending a tyre with her own hands. She wondered whether there might be any work for a beginner, and Leo recognised the shake in her voice and felt a rush of fellow feeling.

Leo invited Tess to sit on the cushioned bench and asked what she hoped to learn and why, and then he did something that a year earlier he would have found difficult: he said nothing at all while she answered. She wanted to understand how things worked, she said, and she wanted a job where, at the end of the day, she could point to something and say that she had made it better. He thought, with a quiet pleasure that surprised him, that this was an excellent beginning for anyone who meant to work with her hands.

Leo did not promise Tess a permanent job, because he could not yet know whether the shop could afford one or whether the two of them would suit each other. He offered her two trial Saturdays at a fair wage, said exactly what he could do and what he could not, and wrote the dates in the small blue notebook in front of her. She watched him do it, and he saw her relax, as people do when somebody speaks plainly.

On her first Saturday a rusty bolt refused to move, and Tess, flushed with frustration and the fear of failing in front of her new employer, very nearly threw her spanner across the shop. Leo crouched beside her and, instead of taking over, showed her how to breathe in for four and out for six, as a certain retired ferry captain had once shown him. The bolt gave way a minute later, with a small defeated squeak, and Tess laughed in astonishment.

At closing time Leo showed Tess how he swept the floor, counted the till and laid out the tools for the first job of the next day. He explained that it was a small present to the person who would arrive in the morning, and he made no speech about it. None was needed, because the following Saturday she did every one of those things before he had finished his tea, and habits, he reflected, are caught far more easily than they are taught.

After two good Saturdays Leo asked Tess to stay on as his apprentice, and she accepted so fast that she interrupted him. He took a white card from the drawer, on which he had copied the first rule in careful handwriting, and passed it across the counter. He explained that the others would follow one at a time, because a rule only helps once it has become a habit, and he realised, as he said it, that he was beginning to sound a little like Ada.

Leo told Ada about Tess and the cards, and she listened with the quiet delight of a captain whose crew has begun to train its own deckhands. The exact words of the rules mattered far less than the habit of returning to them, she said, and nothing would please her more than to see him change them. They were hers because they had suited her, and they would be his only when they suited him.

That evening, over tea on the garden wall, Ada said that Leo had already learned the most important thing, which was to keep returning to the rules. Mean what you say, take one breath before you answer, ask before you decide what is true, and leave every place a little better than you found it: these four, practised imperfectly and often, can steady a whole life. Her last advice was to write his own cards, in his own words, and to keep them where he would see them tomorrow, as the Gull's horn sounded softly across the bay.
